nodes.statement: A defn(simple, undirected) graph G is a pair tuplevertices[G],gEdges[G] where vertices[G] is a set of vertices and gEdges[G] is a set of two-element subsets of vertices[G]. We omit the index G when it is clear from the context. For v,winvertices[G] we write vw as an abbreviation for setv,w. A graph G is defnfinite if its vertex set vertices[G] is finite. Let L be a set and G be a graph. We say that G is defnL-labelled (or just defnlabelled if L is clear from the context) if every vertex in vertices[G] is associated with an element of L, called its defnlabel. We write labelof[G]v to denote the label of the vertex v in G. A graph G' is a defnsubgraph of a graph G, denoted as G'subseteq G iff vertices[G']subseteqvertices[G] and gEdges[G']subseteqgEdges[G]. We say that G' is an defninduced subgraph of G if G' is a subgraph of G and for all v,winvertices[G'], if vwingEdges[G] then vwingEdges[G']. For a graph G we write sizeofvertices[G] for its number of vertices and sizeofgEdges[G] for its number of edges.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:graph}
  A \defn{(simple, undirected) graph} $G$ is a pair
  $\tuple{\vertices[G],\gEdges[G]}$ where $\vertices[G]$ is a set of vertices and $\gEdges[G]$ is a
  set of two-element subsets of $\vertices[G]$. We omit the index $G$ when it
  is clear from the context. For $v,w\in\vertices[G]$ we write $vw$ as an abbreviation
  for $\set{v,w}$. A graph $G$ is \defn{finite} if its vertex set
  $\vertices[G]$ is finite. Let $L$ be a set and $G$ be a graph. We say that
  $G$ is \defn{$L$-labelled} (or just \defn{labelled} if
  $L$ is clear from the context) if every vertex in $\vertices[G]$ is associated
  with an element of $L$, called its \defn{label}. We write
  $\labelof[G]{v}$ to denote the label of the vertex $v$ in $G$. A
  graph $G'$ is a \defn{subgraph} of a graph $G$, denoted as
  $G'\subseteq G$ iff $\vertices[G']\subseteq\vertices[G]$ and $\gEdges[G']\subseteq\gEdges[G]$. We
  say that $G'$ is an \defn{induced subgraph} of $G$ if $G'$ is
  a subgraph of $G$ and for all $v,w\in\vertices[G']$, if $vw\in\gEdges[G]$ then
  $vw\in\gEdges[G']$. For a graph $G$ we write $\sizeof{\vertices[G]}$ for its number of vertices and $\sizeof{\gEdges[G]}$ for its number of edges.

We say that G is defnL-labelled (or just defnlabelled if L is clear from the context) if every vertex in vertices[G] is associated with an element of L, called its defnlabel. We write labelof[G]v to denote the label of the vertex v in G. A graph G' is a defnsubgraph of a graph G, denoted as G'subseteq G iff vertices[G']subseteqvertices[G] and gEdges[G']subseteqgEdges[G]. We say that G' is an defninduced subgraph of G if G' is a subgraph of G and for all v,winvertices[G'], if vwingEdges[G] then vwingEdges[G']. For a graph G we write sizeofvertices[G] for its number of vertices and sizeofgEdges[G] for its number of edges.

nodes.statement: Two graphs G and G' are defnisomorphic if there exists a bijection f colon vertices[G] rightarrow vertices[G'] such that for all v,uinvertices[G] we have vu in gEdges[G] iff f(v)f(u) in gEdges[G'] and labelof[G]v=labelof[G']f(v). We denote this as Gisom[f]G', or simply as Gisom G' if f is clear from the context or not relevant.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:iso}
  Two graphs $G$ and $G'$ are \defn{isomorphic} if there exists a
  bijection $f \colon \vertices[G] \rightarrow \vertices[G']$ such that for all
  $v,u\in\vertices[G]$ we have $vu \in \gEdges[G]$ iff $f(v)f(u) \in \gEdges[G']$ and
  $\labelof[G]{v}=\labelof[G']{f(v)}$. We denote this as
  $G\isom[f]G'$, or simply as $G\isom G'$ if $f$ is clear from the context
  or not relevant.

We denote this as Gisom[f]G', or simply as Gisom G' if f is clear from the context or not relevant.

For a formula $\phi$, we can now define its associated
graph~$\graphof{\phi}$ inductively as follows:
$\graphof\mathord{\circ}=\varnothing$ the empty graph; $\graphof{a}=a$ a 
single-vertex graph whose vertex is labelled by $a$ (by a slight abuse
of notation, we denote that graph also by $a$); similarly
$\graphof{\cneg a}=\cneg a$; finally we define
$\graphof{\phi\vlbin{\parr}\psi}=\graphof{\phi}\vlbin{\parr}\graphof{\psi}$ and
$\graphof{\phi\vlbin{\otimes}\psi}=\graphof{\phi}\vlbin{\otimes}\graphof{\psi}$.

\label{def:graphCompisitionVia}
  Let $G$ be a graph with $n$ vertices $\vertices[G]=\set{v_1,\ldots,v_n}$
  and let $H_1,\ldots,H_n$ be $n$ graphs. We define the
  \defn{composition of $H_1,\ldots,H_n$ via $G$}, denoted as
  $G\connn{H_1,\ldots,H_n}$, by replacing each vertex $v_i$ of $G$
  by the graph $H_i$; and there is an edge between two vertices $x$
  and $y$ if either $x$ and $y$ are in the same $H_i$ and
  $xy\in\gEdges[H_i]$ or $x\in\vertices[H_i]$ and $y\in\vertices[H_j]$ for $i\neq j$ and
  $v_iv_j\in\gEdges[G]$. Formally,
  $G\connn{H_1,\ldots,H_n}=\tuple{V^\ast,E^\ast}$ with
  \begin{equation*}
		V^\ast=\biguplus_{1\le i\le n}\vertices[H_i]
		\quad\quad\mbox{and}\quad\quad
		E^\ast=\left(\biguplus_{1\le i\le n}\gEdges[H_i]\right)\uplus\left\{xy\mid x\in \vertices[H_i],y\in\vertices[H_j],v_iv_j\in\gEdges[G]\right\}
\end{equation*}

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lem:newhope}
  For every non-empty graph $G$ we have exactly one of the following four cases:
  \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
  \item $G$ is a singleton graph.
  \item $G=A\vlbin{\parr}B$ for some $A$, $B$ with $A\neq\varnothing\neq B$.
  \item $G=A\vlbin{\otimes}B$ for some $A$, $B$ with $A\neq\varnothing\neq B$.
  \item $G=P\connn{A_1,\ldots,A_n}$ for some prime graph $P$
    with $n=\sizeof{\vertices[P]}\ge 4$ and $A_i\neq\varnothing$ for every $i\in\set{1,\ldots,n}$.
  \end{enumerate}

Hence vertices[G]=vertices[M_1]cupcdotscupvertices[M_n]. Therefore there is a graph P such that G=PconnnM_1,ldots,M_n. Since all M_i are maximal in G, we can conclude that P is prime. Let $G$ be given. If $\sizeof G=1$, we are in case (i). Now
  assume $\sizeof G>1$, and let $M_1,\ldots,M_n$ be the maximal
  modules of $G$. Note that $n\geq 2$. Now we have two cases:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item For all $i,j\in\set{1,\ldots,n}$ with $i\neq j$ we have
    $M_i\cap M_j=\varnothing$.  Since every vertex of $G$ forms a
    module, every vertex must be part of a maximal module. Hence
    $\vertices[G]=\vertices[M_1]\cup\cdots\cup\vertices[M_n]$. Therefore
    there is a graph $P$ such that
    $G=P\connn{M_1,\ldots,M_n}$. Since all $M_i$ are maximal in
    $G$, we can conclude that $P$ is prime. If $\sizeof{\vertices[P]}\ge 4$
    we are in case (iv). If $\sizeof{\vertices[P]}<4$ we are either in case
    (ii) or (iii), as the two graphs in~\eqref{eq:par-tens} are only
    two prime graphs with $\sizeof{\vertices[P]}=2$, and there are no prime
    graphs with $\sizeof{\vertices[P]}=3$.
  \item We have some $i\neq j$ with $M_i\cap M_j\neq\varnothing$. Let
    $L=M_i\cap M_j$ and $N=M_i\setminus M_j$ and
    $K=M_j\setminus M_i$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:module}, $L$, $N$,
    $K$, and $M_i\cup M_j$ are all modules of $G$. Since $M_i$
    and $M_j$ are maximal, it follows that $G=M_i\cup M_j$, and
    therefore $G=N\vlbin{\otimes} L\vlbin{\otimes} K$ or $G=N\vlbin{\parr} L\vlbin{\parr} K$. \qedhere
  \end{itemize}

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:dual}
  For a graph $G=\tuple{\vertices[G],\gEdges[G]}$, we define its \defn{dual}
  $\cneg G=\tuple{\vertices[G],\gEdges[\cneg G]}$ to have the same set of vertices, and an
  edge $vw\in\gEdges[\cneg G]$ iff $vw\notin\gEdges[G]$ (and $v\neq w$). The label of a vertex $v$ in
  $\cneg G$ is the dual of the label of that vertex in $G$, i.e.,
  $\lnG v = \cneg{\lG v}$. For any two graphs $G$ and $H$, the
  \defn{implication} $G\multimap H$ is defined to be the graph
  $\cneg G\vlbin{\parr}H$.

nodes.statement: The dual graph construction defines the standard De Morgan dualities relating conjunction and disjunction, i.e., for every formula phi, we have graphofcnegphiisomcneggraphofphi. De Morgan dualities extended to prime graphs as cnegPconnnM_1,ldots,M_n isom cnegPconnncnegM_1,ldots,cnegM_n, where cnegP is the dual graph of P. Furthermore, cnegP is prime if and only if P is prime. Thus each pair of prime graphs P and cnegP defines a pair of connectives that are De Morgan duals to each other.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{obs:deMorgan}
The dual graph construction defines the standard De
Morgan dualities relating conjunction and disjunction, i.e., for every
formula $\phi$, we have
$\graphof{\cneg\phi}\isom\cneg{\graphof\phi}$. De Morgan
dualities extended to prime graphs as
$\cneg{P\connn{M_1,\ldots,M_n}} \isom
\cneg{P}\connn{\cneg{M_1},\ldots,\cneg{M_n}}$, where $\cneg{P}$ is
the dual graph of $P$. Furthermore, $\cneg{P}$ is prime if and
only if $P$ is prime. Thus each pair of prime graphs $P$ and
$\cneg{P}$ defines a pair of connectives that are De Morgan duals to
each other.

Furthermore, cnegP is prime if and only if P is prime. Thus each pair of prime graphs P and cnegP defines a pair of connectives that are De Morgan duals to each other.

nodes.statement: As an example, consider the following three graphs: A_1colon c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c vna1 & va1 \\ \\[-1ex] vb1 & vnb1 edgesna1/b1,a1/nb1,na1/nb1,a1/b1 A_2colon c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c vna2 & va2 \\ \\[-1ex] vb2 & vnb2 edgesna2/b2,a2/nb2,na2/nb2 A_3colon c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c vna3 & va3 \\ \\[-1ex] vb3 & vnb3 edgesna3/b3,a3/nb3 The graph A_1 on the left should clearly be provable, as it corresponds to the formula (cneg avlbinparr a)vlbinotimes(bvlbinparrcneg b), which is provable in MLL. The graph A_3 on the right should not be provable, as it corresponds to the formula (cneg avlbinotimes b)vlbinparr(avlbinotimescneg b), which is not provable in MLL. But what about the graph A_2 in the middle? It does not correspond to a formula, and therefore we cannot resort to MLL. Nonetheless, we can make the following observations. If A_2 were provable, then so would be the graph A_4 shown below: A_4colon c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c vna4 & va4 \\ \\[-1ex] va5 & vna5 edgesna4/a5,a4/na5,na4/na5 as it is obtained from A_2 by a simple substitution, i.e., replacing b with a. However, cnegA_4isom A_4, and therefore cnegA_4 and A_4 would both be provable, which would be a contradiction and should be ruled out. Hence, A_2 should not be provable. It also follows that A_1 multimap A_2 cannot hold, as otherwise we would be able to use A_1 and modus ponens to establish that A_2 is provable, which cannot hold as we just observed. By applying a similar argument, we conclude that A_2 multimap A_3 does not hold either.

nodes.statement: An defninference system S is a set of inference rules. We define the set of defnderivations in S inductively below, and we denote a derivation D in S with premise G and conclusion H, as follows: ododdodhGDHS item Every graph G is a derivation (also denoted by G) with premise G and conclusion G. item If G is a graph with n vertices and D_1,dots,D_n are derivations with premise G_i and conclusion H_i for each iinintset1n, then GconnnD_1,dots, D_n is a derivation with premise GconnnG_1,dots, G_n and conclusion GconnnH_1,dots, H_n denoted as strut ododh GConnn ododdodhG_1D_1H_1S ,dots, ododdodhG_nD_nH_nS respectively. If G=vlbinparr or G=vlbinotimes we may respectively write strut ododhododdodhG_1D_1H_1S vlbinparr ododdodhG_2D_2H_2S mboxor ododhododdodhG_1D_1H_1S vlbinotimes ododdodhG_2D_2H_2S item If D_1 is a derivation with premise G_1 and conclusion H_1, and D_2 is a derivation with premise G_2 and conclusion H_2, and vlinfrG_2H_1 is an instance of an inference rule r, then D_2rcomprD_1 is a derivation with premise G_1 and conclusion H_2, denoted as odn odsG_1D_1H_1S r odsG_2D_2H_2S mboxor od oddoddodhG_1D_1odnH_1rG_2 S D_2H_2S mboxor ododdodioddodhG_1 D_1H_1S rG_2 D_2H_2S If H_1isom[f]G_2 we can compose D_1 and D_2 directly to D_2mathopcircD_1, denoted as \; ododo odhodsG_1D_1H_1S f odsG_2D_2H_2S \; mboxor \; ododo odhodsG_1D_1H_1S isom odsG_2D_2H_2S \; mboxor \; ododo odhodsG_1D_1H_1S odsG_2D_2H_2S \; mboxor \; ododdodooddodhG_1 D_1H_1S rG_2 D_2H_2S \; mboxor \; od oddoddodhG_1D_1ododoodhH_1rG_2 S D_2H_2S If f is clear from context we will simply write D_2mathopcircD_1 as hskip5em ododdoddodhG_1 D_1H_1S D_2H_2S mboxor ododdoddodhG_1 D_1G_2S D_2H_2S where we only write H_1 or G_2 in the middle, omitting the isomorphism step, in order to ease readability. However, even if f is not written, we always assume it is part of the derivation and explicitely given. A defnproof in S is a derivation in S whose premise is~varnothing. A graph G is defnprovable in S iff there is a proof in S with conclusion G. We denote this as proves[S]G (or simply as provesG if S is clear from the context). The defnlength of a derivation D, denoted by sizeofD, is the number of inference rule instances in D.

nodes.statement: In order to ease readability of derivations, we will mostly omit the isomorphism steps shown in~, and use the abbreviation~. This concerns also situations as shown below left, which are written as shown below right: ododiodoodiodhA r_1B isomB' r_2C leadsto ododiodiodhA r_1B r_2C mboxor ododiodiodhA r_1B' r_2C In other words, in derivations, we consider graphs equal modulo isomorphisms. In particular, for the length sizeofD of a derivation, we count only the inference steps that are not isomorphisms. This abuse of notation is justified as these isomorphisms can be permuted with all inference rules that we discuss in this paper.   also be checked in linear time.

That is, if G and H are graphs, then glessGH if sizeofvertices[G]<sizeofvertices[H] or if sizeofvertices[G]=sizeofvertices[H] and sizeofgEdges[cneg G]<sizeofgEdges[cneg H].
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:size}
  The \emph{size} of a graph $G$, denoted by $\gsize{G}$, is the
  lexicographic pair $\tuple{\sizeof\vertices[G],\sizeof\gEdges[\cneg G]}$.  That is, if
  $G$ and $H$ are graphs, then $\gless{G}{H}$ if
  $\sizeof{\vertices[G]}<\sizeof{\vertices[H]}$ or if $\sizeof{\vertices[G]}=\sizeof{\vertices[H]}$ and
  $\sizeof{\gEdges[\cneg G]}<\sizeof{\gEdges[\cneg H]}$.

\label{obs:size}
Every
inference rule discussed so far, except for $\mathsf{ai}\mathord{\uparrow}$ and $\mathsf{i}\mathord{\uparrow}$ do
strictly decrease the size of a graph when going bottom-up in a
derivation. That is, whenever we have an instance
${\vlinf{\mathsf{r}}{}{G}{H}}$ of an inference rule
$\mathsf{r}\in\set{\mathsf{ai}\mathord{\downarrow},\mathsf{i}\mathord{\downarrow},\mathsf{s\mkern-1mu.\mkern-1mu sw}\mathord{\downarrow},\mathsf{s\mkern-1mu.\mkern-1mu sw}\mathord{\uparrow},\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow},\mathsf{p}\mathord{\uparrow},\mathsf{g}\mathord{\downarrow},\mathsf{g}\mathord{\uparrow}}$, then
$\gless{H}{G}$.
Since each such inference step either reduces the number of vertices or the number of edges in the dual graph (or both), and these  numbers are  never increased, the length of a derivation in
$\mathsf{GS}$ with conclusion $G$ is bound by $n^2+n$ where $n=\sizeof\vertices[G]$ is
the number of vertices in~$G$.\footnote{For the case that the derivation contains only cographs, it can in fact be shown that the length
    is bound by $\frac12n^2$ (see~\cite{bru:str:swi-med}), but as the details
    are not needed for this paper, we leave them to the reader.}

nodes.statement: The immediate question to address at this point is why we need two cases, where splitting lemmas in the literature require only one case. Notice that Lemma~ is a special case of Lemma~, since vlbinotimes is a prime graph, as indicated in~ in Section~. In the case of the tensor, the two sub-cases of Lemma~ collapse; hence for vlbinotimes the above lemma for prime graphs collapses to the form of Lemma~. The existence of these two separate cases is a surprising novelty since all proof systems, on which the splitting technique has been applied so far, only employ atoms, binary connectives, modalities, and quantifiers. Here, for the first time we present splitting for n-ary connectives with n>2.

The immediate question to address at this point is why we need two cases, where splitting lemmas in the literature require only one case.
Notice that Lemma~\ref{lem:splitting:tens} is a special case of Lemma~\ref{lem:splitting:prime}, since $\vlbin{\otimes}$ is a prime graph, as indicated
in~\eqref{eq:par-tens} in Section~\ref{sec:modules}.
In the case of the tensor, the two sub-cases of Lemma~\ref{lem:splitting:prime} collapse;
hence for $\vlbin{\otimes}$ the above lemma for prime graphs collapses to the form of Lemma~\ref{lem:splitting:tens}.

The existence of these two separate cases is a surprising novelty 
	since all proof systems, on which the splitting technique has been applied so far,

A typical example is given by the following two isomorphic graphs, that are composed differently: vmodule3 c@ \;\;c ve1 & vmodule1 c va1 \\ vb1 vmodule2 c vc1 \\ vd1 edgese1/M1,M3/M2 simeq c@ \;\;c ve1 & vmodule1 c@ \;\;c va1 & vc1 \\ vb1 & vd1 edgese1/M1,a1/d1,b1/d1,a1/c1,b1/c1 This isomorphism is used in the proof below in order to enable the smkern-1mu.mkern-1mu swmathorddownarrow-rule: od odi odi odhvarnothing imathorddownarrow c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c & vnf1 \\ vna1 & & vnc1 \\\\ vnb1 & & vnd1 & vne1 & ve1 & vmodule1 c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c & vf1 \\ va1 & & vc1 \\ vb1 & & vd1 edgese1/M1,nf1/nb1,nf1/nd1,na1/nb1,nc1/nd1,a1/d1,b1/d1,a1/c1,b1/c1,f1/a1,f1/c1 smkern-1mu.mkern-1mu swmathorddownarrow c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c & vnf1 \\ vna1 & & vnc1 \\\\ vnb1 & & vnd1 & vne1 & vf1 & vmodule3 c@ \;\;c ve1 & vmodule1 c va1 \\ vb1 vmodule2 c vc1 \\ vd1 edgese1/M1,M3/M2,nf1/nb1,nf1/nd1,na1/nb1,nc1/nd1 We can apply splitting to the above graph in various ways. One possibility is to apply splitting to the tensor on the right as shown in the conclusion of the above proof. For that we appeal to Case~ in the proof of Lemma~, which firstly observes that there is a proof of cnege vlbinparr e and a proof of the following induced sub-graph. c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c c@ \;\;c@ \;\;c vna1 & vnf1 & vnc1 \\\\ vnb1 & & vnd1 & vf1 & vmodule1 c va1 \\ vb1 vmodule2 c vc1 \\ vd1 edgesM1/M2,nf1/nb1,nf1/nd1,na1/nb1,nc1/nd1 Case~ is then used to renormalise the proof of~ such that the P_5 on the left is split into two parts, from which we can reassemble a proof of the graph in the conclusion of~ which satisfies the conditions of splitting for the tensor that we selected. In particular, if A = e vlbinotimes (a vlbinparr b) and B = c vlbinparr d in Lemma~, then we obtain K_A = (cnega vlbinotimes cnegb) vlbinparr cnege and K_B = cnegc vlbinparr cnegd, as required (the context is empty for this example).

nodes.statement: A prime graph P is a defnconnector of a graph G if P occurs in the modular decomposition of G. A defnsubconnector of G is a prime graph that is an induced subgraph of a connector of~G.
nodes.raw_latex:
A prime graph $P$ is a \defn{connector} of a graph $G$ 
if $P$ occurs in the modular decomposition of $G$.
A \defn{subconnector} of $G$ is a prime graph that is an induced subgraph of a connector of~$G$.
nodes.clean_text: A prime graph P is a defnconnector of a graph G if P occurs in the modular decomposition of G. A defnsubconnector of G is a prime graph that is an induced subgraph of a connector of~G.

nodes.statement: The graph from Example~ has three occurrences of the connector P_4, one occurrence of the connector vlbinotimes and one occurrence of the connector vlbinparr. Note that vlbinotimes is a subconnector of any graph containing at least one edge, and vlbinparr is a subconnector of any graph containing two distinct vertices u and v that are not connected by an edge in G. nodes.statement: Let G be a graph that is provable in GScupsetsmkern-1mu.mkern-1mu swmathorduparrow. Then G admits a derivation tildeD in GScupsetsmkern-1mu.mkern-1mu swmathorduparrow such that every connector of a graph occurring in tildeD is a subconnector of G.
assumptions: Let G be a graph that is provable in GScupsetsmkern-1mu.mkern-1mu swmathorduparrow.
conclusions: Then G admits a derivation tildeD in GScupsetsmkern-1mu.mkern-1mu swmathorduparrow such that every connector of a graph occurring in tildeD is a subconnector of G.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{thm:anaCon}
  Let $G$ be a graph that is provable in $\mathsf{GS}\cup\set{\mathsf{s\mkern-1mu.\mkern-1mu sw}\mathord{\uparrow}}$.
  Then $G$ admits a derivation $\tilde{\mathcal{D}}$ in $\mathsf{GS}\cup\set{\mathsf{s\mkern-1mu.\mkern-1mu sw}\mathord{\uparrow}}$ 
  such that every connector of a graph occurring in $\tilde{\mathcal{D}}$ is a subconnector of $G$.

nodes.label: thm:anaCon

nodes.statement: Let G be given, and let D be a derivation of G in GScupsetsmkern-1mu.mkern-1mu swmathorduparrow. We are now going to transform D into a derivation tildeD that does not contain any occurrences of a connector that is not a subconnector of G. Let P be such a connector occuring in D. While going up in the derivation D, only an instance of smkern-1mu.mkern-1mu swmathorddownarrow can introduce P as connector, i.e., the premise of the rule instance contains the prime graph P as connector, but the conclusion does not. This happens by moving a module M_i inside a context CCoonsPconnnM_1, ldots, M_i-1, varnothing, M_i+1, ldots, M_nR where M_1, dots,M_i-1,M_i+1, dots, M_n are non-empty. As the premise of the derivation D is empty, this occurrence of P must be destroyed eventually, i.e., D contains a rule instance whose conclusion contains P as connector, but the premise does not. This can be done via an instance of smkern-1mu.mkern-1mu swmathorduparrow, pmathorddownarrow, or aimathorddownarrow. Below, we will list all cases how this can happen, and show how the derivation can be rewritten without introducing and destroying this occurrence of P. For this, we proceed by induction on the multiset multisetP_1,ldots,P_n, where P_1,ldots,P_n are the occurrences of connectors in D that are not subconnectors of G, and where we use the multiset ordering: Q

nodes.statement: We call a generalised formula a formula that is generated by a countable set of positive or negative propositional atoms seta,cnega,b,cneg b,ldots via the following grammar: phi , psi Coloneqq a mid cneg amid phi vlbinparr psi mid phi vlbinotimes psi mid mathsf C(phi_1,dots, phi_n) where mathsf Cin mathcal C is any n-ary connective.
nodes.raw_latex:
We call a \emph{generalised formula} a formula that is generated by a countable set of positive or negative propositional atoms $\set{a,\cneg{a},b,\cneg b,\ldots}$ via the following grammar:
$$
\phi , \psi \Coloneqq a \mid \cneg a\mid \phi \vlbin{\parr} \psi \mid \phi \vlbin{\otimes} \psi \mid \mathsf C(\phi_1,\dots, \phi_n)
$$

We show that the first sequent is not provable. The same reasoning applies to the other sequents.
In a derivation of $\mathsf{G_4}(a,b,c,d),  \cneg c\vlbin{\parr} (\cneg d\vlbin{\otimes} (\cneg a \vlbin{\parr} \cneg b))$ we can apply as first rule a $\vlbin{\parr}$.
Any derivation continuing with a $\vlbin{\otimes}$ rule must have in one branch $\mathsf{G_4}(a,b,c,d)$  and either $\cneg d$ or $\cneg a \vlbin{\parr} \cneg b$. This makes it impossible to match all pairs of dual atoms in axioms. 
Similarly,  starting with one of the two $\mathsf{G_4}$ rules in \ref{eq:G4rules}, 
or starting with the $\vlbin{\parr}$ rule followed by one of these two rules, 
we encounter the same problem
of mismatched  atoms.

Both $\mathsf{MLL}^\circ_{\mathcal C}$ (by definition) and $\mathsf{GS}$ (by Corollary~\ref{cor:MLL}) are {conservative} extensions of $\mathsf{MLL}$.
The non $\vlbin{\otimes}/\vlbin{\parr}$-decomposable $4$-ary connective $\mathsf{G_4}$  should  be translated as a non-decomposable graph with $4$ vertices, that is, a $\mathsf{P_4}$.
Thus, the translation of $\mathsf{G_4}(a,b,c,d)$ should be of the shape $\mathsf{P_4}\connn{\sigma(a),\sigma(b),\sigma(c),\sigma(d)}$ for some permutation $\sigma$ over the set $\set{a,b,c,d}$.
However for each possible translation of $\mathsf{G_4}$, one of the  implications in  \eqref{eq:non-provableMLLG}, which are not derivable in $\mathsf{MLL}^\circ_{\mathcal C}$ and contain $\mathsf{G_4}$,
is translated into a $\mathsf{GS}$-derivable implication.
We can conclude that the systems $\mathsf{MLL}^\circ_{\mathcal C}$ and $\mathsf{GS}$ are not equivalent.

nodes.statement: In the connectives-as-partitions setting, a generalised n-ary connective described by a partition Psubsetpartof n is decomposable if there is a vlbinotimes/vlbinparr-formula F such that P is the set of partitions associated to all possible derivations of F .
nodes.raw_latex:
In the connectives-as-partitions setting, a generalised $n$-ary connective described by a partition $P\subset\partof n$ is \emph{decomposable} if there is a $\vlbin{\otimes}/\vlbin{\parr}$-formula $F$ such that $P$ is 
the set of partitions associated to all possible derivations of $F$ \cite{danos:regnier:89,acc:mai:20}.

nodes.statement: In addition, in this concurrency scenario, we assume that the information flow is strictly managed such that, although information can flow via x from c to a, and from a to d via y, those information flows must be strictly separated, and therefore a must be trusted or designed such that the information from c does not flow to d indirectly via a.

such that, although information can flow via $x$ from $c$ to $a$, and from $a$ to $d$ via $y$,
those information flows must be strictly separated, and therefore $a$ must be trusted or designed such that the information from $c$ does not flow to $d$ indirectly via $a$.
